{"id": "13:9/q06", "question": "What does al-kabīr mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether greatness is explained chiefly through rank and majesty, sovereign power, knowledge, incomparability, or inward effects.", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q06/p1", "position": "God is supremely great in majesty and rank, with everything else beneath Him.", "reasons": "Muqatil says none is greater; Wahidi says divine rank and entitlement to exalted attributes make every other greatness small; Ibn Atiyya calls it unrestricted majesty; Ibn al-Jawzi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Elmalili combine rank with the inferiority of everything else. Damghani glosses it great or majestic and notes 4:34. Ibn Ashur explains figurative size and multitude as established metaphors for abstract majesty; Tabatabai likewise traces the word from bodily size to God's possession and encompassing of every perfection, with more beyond. Al-Harali in Biqai describes the evident disparity of degree: only God has absolute greatness, and human pretensions end in humiliation at resurrection. Ibn Kathir says He is greater than all."}, {"id": "13:9/q06/p2", "position": "God is the sovereign, master, and one able to do all things.", "reasons": "Nahhas and Tabrisi give sovereignty and omnipotence; Razi says greatness cannot refer to bodily size or volume and instead denotes power and divine measures."}, {"id": "13:9/q06/p3", "position": "His greatness entails that nothing escapes His knowledge.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Bursevi link majesty to all-encompassing knowledge; Bursevi also calls Him majestic in status."}, {"id": "13:9/q06/p4", "position": "His perfect attributes place everything beneath Him and beyond resemblance to creatures.", "reasons": "Tabrisi gives this as an alternative; Ibn al-Jawzi adds that God is unlike created things. Alusi reports an interpretation of both names as disavowing creaturely traits ascribed by unbelievers, citing 37:159."}, {"id": "13:9/q06/p5", "position": "He encompasses all capacities and unfailingly grants each its due.", "reasons": "Qashani reads greatness as never failing to supply what a capacity requires."}, {"id": "13:9/q06/p6", "position": "His greatness fills gnostics' hearts, making all else small.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar's inward explanation is reported by Sulami; Ibn Ata says God is great in essence."}]}
{"id": "13:9/q07", "question": "What does al-mutaʿāl mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether exaltation is explained as sovereign power, transcendence from created traits, absolute inaccessibility, or an inward account of divine giving.", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q07/p1", "position": "God is exalted above all creation and all things by unrivaled power and dominion.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Thalabi, Baghawi, Tabrisi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Baydawi, Bursevi and Elmalili stress power over all; Tabari says all things, Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Khattabi's 'above creation,' and Tabrisi adds no equal. Jishumi says al-mutaʿāl and al-ʿālī are synonymous or denote incomparable power; Tabrisi reports the same equivalence and an omnipotence no equal shares. Ibn Kathir adds all-subduing power, before which all submit. Tabatabai distinguishes ʿAlī as above and ruling all from mutaʿāl as ultimate height dominating from every direction. Ibn Ashur gives complete invincibility, citing 16:3, as one explanation."}, {"id": "13:9/q07/p2", "position": "God transcends created attributes, defects, impermissible descriptions, and polytheists' claims.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan in Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi specifies the polytheists' sayings; al-Azhari specifies heretics' impiety. Razi extends transcendence to all that is impermissible in essence, attributes and acts; Tabrisi likewise covers acts and polytheist claims. Ibn al-Jawzi and Nasafi mention creaturely attributes; Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, al-Kawashi in Bursevi, and Elmalili concur. Ibn Ashur gives freedom from deficiencies as an alternative. Alusi reports both names understood against disbelievers' creaturely descriptions, citing 37:159."}, {"id": "13:9/q07/p3", "position": "God's elevation is absolute, beyond approach, comprehension, definition, or comparison.", "reasons": "Jishumi says He surpasses every account; Biqai says no approach in essence, attribute or action, while al-Harali says no judgment or proof reaches Him: imagined arguments fall before His decisive proof, and He is exalted in knowledge, judgment and argument, citing 42:16 and 6:149. Alusi names essence, knowledge and every attribute. Asad calls His exaltedness infinite over everything existing or possible, cites 6:100, and records Zamakhshari's point about human definitions. Asad notes this divine attribute occurs only here in the Qur'an. Tabatabai describes height surpassing all heights."}, {"id": "13:9/q07/p4", "position": "His continuous effusion gives full gifts as soon as readiness arises.", "reasons": "Qashani says God neither delays once a capacity is ready nor gives less than it requires."}, {"id": "13:9/q07/p5", "position": "Approach to Him depends entirely on His generosity.", "reasons": "Jaʿfar, reported by Sulami, offers this inward sense; Ibn Ata describes Him as exalted in attributes."}]}
{"id": "13:9/q08", "question": "What does the form of al-mutaʿāl convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q08/p1", "position": "It derives from ʿuluww, elevation, in the mutafāʿil or tafaʿul form.", "reasons": "Tabari compares al-mutaqārib from qurb and al-mutadānī from dunūw; Ibn Atiyya derives it from elevation. Ibn Ashur says tafaʿul makes exaltation inherent and necessary rather than conferred; Biqai says the reciprocal form intensifies transcendence. Tabatabai compares the intensive absolute object 'greatly exalted' in 17:43. Jishumi and Tabrisi also report its equivalence to al-ʿālī."}]}
{"id": "13:9/q09", "question": "How is the final yāʾ of al-mutaʿāl read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted reader and route, regular morphology versus rasm and verse cadence, and disputed reports from Qunbul and Warsh.", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q09/p1", "position": "It is retained in both connected reading and pause.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid names Ibn Kathir and two Abu Amr transmissions; Jishumi and Nashr also name Yaʿqub. Wahidi calls retention the regular form and cites Sibawayh: the definite article favors keeping yāʾ at pause because it survives connection, unlike indefinite qadin. Ibn Atiyya prefers it as regular; Ibn al-Jazari prefers established practice and trusted Qunbul reports over disputed extra-yāʾ reports, against al-Dani's judgment of error. Nashr says both Ibn Kathir transmissions affirm it, despite conflicting Qunbul reports. Qiraat-ER says this completes the active participle morphologically without changing meaning."}, {"id": "13:9/q09/p2", "position": "It is omitted in both connection and pause.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid, Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Ibn al-Jawzi, Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin attribute omission to the other readers; Jishumi and Razi cite ease, while Abu Hayyan and al-Samin note agreement with the written form. Sibawayh, cited by Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin, allows loss at verse endings by analogy to rhyme and indefinite forms, though he regards loss in connected speech as unexpected or poor; Ibn Atiyya adds that tanwin alternates with the definite article. Nahhas and Ibn Ashur cite verse endings, Ibn Ashur noting the cadence of wāl and al-āṣāl (13:11, 13:15) and that retention is more analogical while omission is common Arabic. Nashr records Qunbul reports of omission in both, including a Shanbudh route, but Ibn al-Jazari adopts affirmation."}, {"id": "13:9/q09/p3", "position": "It is retained at pause but omitted in connection.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports this from Ibn Shanabudh through Qunbul, alongside the other readers' complete omission."}, {"id": "13:9/q09/p4", "position": "A Qunbul report omits it at pause only.", "reasons": "Nashr records this as a conflicting report alongside complete omission, while Ibn al-Jazari chooses affirmation in both states."}, {"id": "13:9/q09/p5", "position": "Warsh may retain or omit yāʾ at pause in this category.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports al-Azraq's account of Warsh's choice for indefinite, declinable words in this category."}]}
{"id": "13:9/q10", "question": "What does the pairing of divine knowledge, greatness, and exaltation convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the two names chiefly reinforce universal knowledge and power or jointly negate false creaturely descriptions.", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q10/p1", "position": "Knowledge, greatness, and power together mean nothing escapes or overcomes God.", "reasons": "Tabatabai says the combination signals total encompassing and dominance. Al-Tibi in Alusi says the names add greatness and power to knowledge, countering Christian and polytheist claims; he connects this with 13:8. Biqai says preceding descriptions exhaust what human reason can bear, while the reality is absolute greatness and transcendence. Sulami's Ibn Ata says true knowledge belongs to God, great in essence and exalted in attributes."}, {"id": "13:9/q10/p2", "position": "Both names jointly reject created attributes ascribed to God by disbelievers.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this alternative with 37:159; al-Tibi's explanation also names Christian and polytheist claims."}]}

Biqai compares resurrection to first creation and says distinguishing scattered dust is less astonishing than distinguishing reproductive fluid from mixed water."}, {"id": "13:9/q11/p3", "position": "Requested signs are withheld because the requesters are obstinate or because the signs would not benefit them.", "reasons": "Kashshaf says differing signs are deliberate wisdom and God would grant the requested sign were it beneficial. {"id": "13:9/q12", "question": "How does this verse serve the sūra's overall purpose?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q12/p1", "position": "It supports the sūra's portrayal of true revelation whose effects vary with its recipients.", "reasons": "Biqai compares revelation's sound and fame with thunder: it may guide or leave hearers blind, as lightning and rain may help, fail or harm according to where they fall."}]}
{"id": "13:9/q13", "question": "What revelation setting is given for this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q13/p1", "position": "The entire sūra is Makkan, with no Madinan verse.", "reasons": "Islahi rejects the codices' Madinan classification in favor of this account."}]}
{"id": "13:9/q14", "question": "What are tafsīr and taʾwīl, and how do they differ?", "turns_on": "The source of interpretation, degree of certainty, unit of explanation, current usage, and etymology.", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q14/p1", "position": "They are synonymous.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this view from Abu Ubayda."}, {"id": "13:9/q14/p2", "position": "Tafsīr is broader and mainly explains words; taʾwīl treats meanings and whole constructions in divine books.", "reasons": "Alusi reports al-Raghib: tafsir applies to divine and other books, ta'wil to divine books specifically."}, {"id": "13:9/q14/p3", "position": "Tafsīr asserts God's intended meaning decisively; taʾwīl prefers a possible meaning without certainty.", "reasons": "Alusi attributes this distinction to al-Maturidi."}, {"id": "13:9/q14/p4", "position": "Tafsīr relies on transmitted reports; taʾwīl relies on reasoned analysis.", "reasons": "Alusi records this as another proposed distinction."}, {"id": "13:9/q14/p5", "position": "In current usage taʾwīl often means spiritual allusions and unveiled insights.", "reasons": "Alusi says earlier conventional definitions do not match this usage; if distinctions are meant literally, they require reconsideration, although every unveiling involves a return and every return an unveiling."}, {"id": "13:9/q14/p6", "position": "Taʾwīl derives from 'return,' not from siyāsa, 'management.'", "reasons": "Alusi rejects deriving it from the interpreter directing speech and placing its meaning."}]}
{"id": "13:9/q15", "question": "Why is Qur'anic interpretation necessary?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q15/p1", "position": "The Qur'an's guidance and rulings require explanation and God's enabling grace to understand.", "reasons": "Alusi calls legal rulings the basis of enduring happiness and the straight path. Even eloquent Companions repeatedly asked the Prophet and sometimes misunderstood, as Adi ibn Hatim did the white and black thread in 2:187; present readers need interpretation at least as much."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q01", "question": "What does equality here say about God's knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired descriptions are a general contrast or describe one person's concealed wrongdoing.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q01/p1", "position": "Secret and open speech, night concealment and daytime exposure are equally known to God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, and others extend the contrast to hidden and witnessed deeds. Ibn Kathīr cites 20:7, 27:25, 11:5 and 10:61, and ʿĀʾisha's report that she missed part of a woman's plea which God heard (58:1). Al-Qurṭubī and al-Māwardī specify good and evil. Al-Rāzī and al-Bayḍāwī stress comprehensive knowledge; human sight is obscured by night (al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī)."}, {"id": "13:10/q01/p2", "position": "The paired figures are sinful in secret at night and overt by day, yet neither state hides sin from God.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the same sin is hidden then spread. Mujāhid and al-Rāzī also describe sins committed openly by day. Al-Wāḥidī notes this requires supplying 'sins' in both clauses. Ibn ʿAṭiyya extends the analysis to deeds; al-Kāshifī includes speech and acts. Asad reports Ibn ʿAbbās, via al-Baghawī and al-Rāzī, as taking daytime going forth to be open evil deeds."}, {"id": "13:10/q01/p3", "position": "The verse specifically exposes a suspicious person who sins at night but presents himself as innocent by day.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid identify one person; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers this reading and argues that omission of a second man otherwise occurs only in poetry. Al-Ālūsī dismisses Ibn ʿAṭiyya's three-class version."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q02", "question": "How does sawāʾ govern the sentence?", "turns_on": "Whether sawāʾ is predicate or subject, and whether its verbal-noun sense needs an omitted possessive.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q02/p1", "position": "Sawāʾ is a fronted predicate; the two relative expressions are its delayed subject in the nominative.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj say equality requires two terms. Al-Ṭabarī makes the first man subject and the others coordinated. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī say sawāʾ remains singular because it began as a verbal noun; Abū Zayd attests a dual form. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports the alternative ordering."}, {"id": "13:10/q02/p2", "position": "Sawāʾ is a verbal noun whose predication requires an omitted 'possessors of equality'.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says verbal nouns cannot directly govern nouns as participles do; al-Khansāʾ's verse illustrates an omitted possessive. Al-Naḥḥās reports Abū Isḥāq's analogy with 'a man of justice'; al-Ṭabrisī and al-Rāzī repeat it."}, {"id": "13:10/q02/p3", "position": "Sawāʾ functions as an adjective meaning 'equal' without ellipsis.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says frequent use made the verbal noun participial; Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares ʿadl, zawr and ḍayf. Abū Bakr prefers overt syntax without an omitted noun. Sībawayh objects to beginning with an indefinite participle, a point reported by al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī."}, {"id": "13:10/q02/p4", "position": "Sawāʾ is the subject, qualified by minkum, with the following expression filling its predicate slot.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says the predicate is delayed. Al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān cite Sībawayh's example 'good and evil are equal to him'; al-Samīn disputes Ibn ʿAṭiyya's report that Sībawayh rejected this indefinite opening. Al-Naḥḥās cites Ḥassān's poem for the equality in standing before God of insult, praise and defense of the Messenger."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q03", "question": "How is minkum attached?", "turns_on": "Which constituent the prepositional phrase limits.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q03/p1", "position": "Minkum is circumstantial to the implicit subject of sawāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī use sawāʾ's sense 'equal'; Abū al-Baqāʾ and al-Ālūsī bar attaching it to the hidden subject of asarra or jahara because that would front an element of a relative clause."}, {"id": "13:10/q03/p2", "position": "Minkum qualifies sawāʾ or attaches to it in the sense 'equal among you'.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports both formulations; the latter compares the construction 'I passed by Zayd'. Al-Samīn reports the subject parse is licensed by this qualification."}, {"id": "13:10/q03/p3", "position": "Minkum is understood separately after both speakers: the secret speaker among you and the open speaker among you.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī supplies the repeated phrase after each clause."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q04", "question": "What are secret and public qawl?", "turns_on": "Whether concealed qawl is inward thought, a very quiet utterance, or an inward state of knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q04/p1", "position": "Secret speech is inward or self-addressed, and public speech is voiced to another.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Zajjāj give this contrast. Al-Ālūsī also allows an utterance so quiet only its speaker hears it; public speech contrasts with both senses."}, {"id": "13:10/q04/p2", "position": "Qawl can mean an unspoken idea or thought here.", "reasons": "Asad says the literal meaning is utterance, but figurative usage includes an idea merely conceived; al-ʿĀshūr's context and Abū Ḥayyān's specification concern hidden and spoken words."}, {"id": "13:10/q04/p3", "position": "The contrast is between latent knowledge and knowledge brought from potentiality into actuality.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads inner speech and public speech as stages of manifestation."}]}

{"id": "13:10/q06", "question": "What does sārib by day mean?", "turns_on": "Whether saraba denotes movement into public view or into cover, and which sense fits day.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q06/p1", "position": "A person going along a road or about his affairs, visibly and freely by day.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj and later lexicographers relate sarb to a path. Al-Māwardī distinguishes evening sarūb from morning sarūj. Ibn ʿĀshūr derives the verb from the concrete road noun. Arab linguists differ on fatḥa versus kasra for the sīn in āmin fī sirbihi, al-Ṭabarī reports."}, {"id": "13:10/q06/p2", "position": "Sārib is literally one appearing or emerging into view.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī derives it from saraba 'appear, come out' and quotes Qays at night. Al-Ṭabrisī reports al-Ḥasan's account of concealment both night and day."}, {"id": "13:10/q06/p4", "position": "Related sarb usage denotes flowing water from a waterskin.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī cites Dhū al-Rumma for the flowing-water sense; al-Qutaybī compares the quick errand-runner to water flowing away."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q07", "question": "How are the night-hidden and day-traveling descriptions joined?", "turns_on": "Whether the final adjective coordinates with a person, an adjective, or an omitted relative.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q07/p1", "position": "Sārib coordinates with the whole man huwa mustakhfin phrase or with man, contrasting two people.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī give this parse. Al-Ālūsī says huwa makes the first description explicit and the matching description before sārib is omitted. The author of al-Kashf says the generic relative and descriptive forms coincide, with the descriptive form more explicit; a definite referent would suggest an unintended implication."}, {"id": "13:10/q07/p2", "position": "Sārib coordinates with mustakhfin, while man covers two people by sense.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī illustrates a dual man with a line about two companions; al-Samīn says the wolf line coordinates on sense alone and criticizes al-Zamakhsharī's wording. Al-Burhān compares 37:164."}, {"id": "13:10/q07/p4", "position": "The absence of repeated man favors one person or one category who rests at night and travels by day.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says otherwise man would have to be deleted, a move he finds only in poetry; Abū Ḥayyān reports his view. Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid read the two moments as one person's conduct."}, {"id": "13:10/q07/p5", "position": "The wording may enumerate three classes: secret speaker, public speaker, and a person who changes conduct between night and day.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya supplies sin and apparent innocence for the third class. {"id": "13:10/q08", "question": "Why pair secrecy with night and open movement with day?", "turns_on": "Whether the pairing explains natural visibility or serves intensified rhetorical contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q08/p1", "position": "Night is naturally more concealing and daylight makes movement more visible, sharpening the equal-knowledge contrast.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, Abū Bakr, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and al-Ālūsī use this fit against the reversed gloss. Al-Biqāʿī calls the omitted counterparts iḥtibāk; al-Burhān identifies antithesis and cites 3:26 and 35:19–22."}, {"id": "13:10/q08/p2", "position": "The contrast stretches knowledge beyond human plausibility, a rhetorical hyperbole only relative to listeners.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān defines hyperbole as intensification beyond ordinary mental expectation and says divine knowledge itself is not exaggerated."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q09", "question": "Does the wording carry a warning or practical lesson?", "turns_on": "The moral application drawn from God's knowledge.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q09/p1", "position": "Awareness of God's knowledge calls for vigilance and self-accounting.", "reasons": "Study Quran urges scrutiny of actions, thoughts and heart, and reports ʿUmar's instruction to take oneself to account before judgment."}, {"id": "13:10/q09/p2", "position": "No wrongdoer can hide from God's grasp or make Him act hastily.", "reasons": "Islāḥī connects equal knowledge of deeds and thoughts with God's ability to seize wrongdoers at His chosen time. {"id": "13:10/q16", "question": "Is seeking refuge obligatory before Qur'an recitation?", "turns_on": "Whether the command and prophetic practice establish recurring obligation, one-time obligation or recommendation.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q16/p1", "position": "It is obligatory every time, inside or outside prayer.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ invokes the Prophet's constant practice and 7:158, the command of 16:98 recurring with every recitation, the obligation to repel Satan, and precaution."}, {"id": "13:10/q16/p2", "position": "One recitation in a lifetime discharges the obligation.", "reasons": "Ibn Sīrīn gives this limited obligatory view."}, {"id": "13:10/q16/p3", "position": "It is recommended, not obligatory.", "reasons": "The majority cite the Prophet's omission of the formula in teaching a Bedouin prayer, though an objection says that teaching was not exhaustive. {"id": "13:10/q17", "question": "Should the refuge formula be recited quietly or aloud?", "turns_on": "Whether precedent or analogy to the opening supplication guides the choice.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q17/p1", "position": "Either manner is permitted, with loud recitation preferred in al-Shāfiʿī's al-Imlāʾ.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī cites Ibn ʿUmar's quiet practice and Abū Hurayra's aloud practice."}, {"id": "13:10/q17/p2", "position": "Quiet recitation is favored.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares the formula to the opening supplication rather than al-Fātiḥa and treats loudness as an added quality."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q18", "question": "How may non-scriptural sciences relate to Qur'anic interpretation?", "turns_on": "Which disciplines the Qur'an contains, assists, alludes to or leaves aside.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q18/p1", "position": "The Qur'an includes prophetic histories, ethics, jurisprudence, law, creed, legal theory, Arabic and rhetoric.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls these first-level sciences contained in it."}, {"id": "13:10/q18/p2", "position": "Wisdom, astronomy and the properties of created things can broaden an exegete's knowledge.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr's second level describes helpful background disciplines."}, {"id": "13:10/q18/p3", "position": "Earth strata, medicine and logic may be alluded to by or support the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr's third level admits supporting or alluded-to fields."}, {"id": "13:10/q18/p4", "position": "Divination, augury, mythology, prosody and rhyme do not serve interpretation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr's fourth level includes invalid arts and fields without interpretive use."}, {"id": "13:10/q18/p5", "position": "Philosophical sciences should not be reconciled with Qur'anic meanings because of doctrinal error.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī argues against this reconciliation; Ibn ʿĀshūr says his contempt for philosophers goes too far."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q19", "question": "Was Sūrat al-Raʿd wholly revealed in Mecca?", "turns_on": "The classification of the sūra's place of revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q19/p1", "position": "The whole sūra is Makkan, with no Madinan verse.", "reasons": "Islāḥī rejects the codices' Madinan classification."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q20", "question": "What is the sūra's governing aim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q20/p1", "position": "It portrays revelation as intrinsically true, while its heard force leads some to guidance and leaves others blind or astray.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī likens this variation to thunder, lightning and rain benefiting, failing or harming according to where they fall."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q21", "question": "Can one person possess both innate perfection and acquired excellence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q21/p1", "position": "Only figuratively: innate perfection and excellence won through effort and removal of vices are distinct.", "reasons": "Al-Uqlīshī distinguishes intellect, character and conduct from acquired moral development."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q22", "question": "What is the scope of divine knowledge compared with human knowledge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q22/p1", "position": "God's knowledge is infinite, complete and certain through every stage of life; human knowledge is limited and changeable.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu traces the contrast from conception to death; al-Māwardī and al-Ṭabrisī mention human inability to see nighttime states."}]}
{"id": "13:10/q23", "question": "What do appointed angels do in the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "13:10/q23/p1", "position": "Angels appointed by God watch over people.", "reasons": "Islāḥī states their role; Ibn Zayd's ʿĀmir-Arbad story links their protection to 13:10–11."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q01", "question": "What do the opening letters signify?", "turns_on": "Whether the letters name the sura or alphabet, encode divine declarations, or point to the Quran's composition and inimitability.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q01/p1", "position": "They are disjoined letter names serving as an opening or name of the sura or Quran.", "reasons": "Majaz calls them unvoweled letter names; al-Hasan reports companions using such openings as sura names and keys; al-Kashifi reports them as names of the Quran. Ibn Atiyya, Tabarsi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, Qurtubi, Asad, Islahi and Study Quran refer to earlier discussions; Kuran Yolu names them huruf al-muqatta'a."}, {"id": "14:1/q01/p2", "position": "They encode divine names or declarations.", "reasons": "Abu Salih and Ata give 'I am God, the Merciful'; Wahidi Wajiz and Ibn Abbas give 'I am God who sees'; Jishumi also reports derivation from God's names and attributes."}, {"id": "14:1/q01/p3", "position": "They demonstrate the Quran's inimitability using the Arabs' familiar letters.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim argues that people know the component letters yet cannot match the Quran. {"id": "14:1/q02", "question": "How are the opening letters and 'Book' construed grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the initials form a syntactic subject and whether an omitted demonstrative, qualifier, or verb is supplied.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q02/p1", "position": "'Book' predicates an omitted 'this is'; the revealed clause describes it.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya and others supply hādhā. {"id": "14:1/q05", "question": "How does 'We sent it down to you' attach and what does its wording convey?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause is descriptive, predicative, or explanatory.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q05/p1", "position": "The revelation clause qualifies 'Book'.", "reasons": "Nahas, Wahidi and Ibn Atiyya make it adjectival; Wahidi compares 'Zayd is a man I sent to you.' {"id": "14:1/q06", "question": "What does attributing the Book's descent to God imply about divine speech?", "turns_on": "Whether descent is predicated of eternal divine speech itself or its conveyed meanings or letters.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q06/p1", "position": "What descends is conveyed meaning or originated letters, not God's eternal attribute itself.", "reasons": "Al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib and Abu al-Ma'ali distinguish conveyed meanings from eternal speech; Razi answers the Mu'tazilites that Quranic letters are originated, which no one disputes."}, {"id": "14:1/q06/p2", "position": "The described descent shows the thing sent down cannot be eternal.", "reasons": "Razi reports this Mu'tazilite argument and replies that the originated letters are the thing described."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q07", "question": "How does the wording honor the Prophet?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q07/p1", "position": "The majestic plural, direct address, and attribution of bringing people out honor his role.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi highlight the plural and direct address; Ibn Atiyya says the honor lies in naming his invitation and warning although God creates guidance."}, {"id": "14:1/q07/p2", "position": "Muhammad's favor over angels includes a promise of forgiveness.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas compares the threat against an angel claiming divinity in 21:29 with the Prophet's forgiveness in 48:2."}]}
{"id": "14:1/q08", "question": "What does the lām of 'so that you bring out' express?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause states the intended end of revelation or a consequence that actually occurs to all.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q08/p1", "position": "It marks the purpose of sending the Book.", "reasons": "Nahas paraphrases 'so that people may come out'; Wahidi, Samin and Alusi attach it to anzalna. {"id": "14:1/q09", "question": "Does the purpose clause imply that divine acts have purposes?", "turns_on": "Whether benefit governs or compels divine action, or divine purposes are affirmed as benefits for creatures.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q09/p1", "position": "God's acts and commands have beneficial purposes for creatures.", "reasons": "Razi reports Mu'tazilite inference from the lām; Ibn al-Qayyim and others cite over ten thousand apparent scriptural examples and call it the Salaf view, which Alusi finds persuasive. {"id": "14:1/q10", "question": "What is the variant reading of the purpose verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q10/p1", "position": "A reported reading has third-person yāʾ, li-yukhrij, with al-nās nominative as subject.", "reasons": "Kashshaf reports li-yukhrija al-nas; Samin and Abu Hayyan specify the nominative subject. {"id": "14:1/q12", "question": "What does the Prophet do in bringing people out?", "turns_on": "Whether the Messenger's guidance is an indispensable source of knowledge, an alert to proof, or a mediated call under God's guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q12/p1", "position": "He guides instrumentally by reciting, calling, explaining, and warning; God grants or creates the guidance.", "reasons": "Tabari distinguishes divine granting of faith from prophetic explanation; Jishumi calls the attribution figurative. {"id": "14:1/q13", "question": "What does bringing people from darkness into light mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair denotes core unbelief and faith or more specific kinds of ignorance, doubt, innovation, and conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q13/p1", "position": "It is a move from unbelief, idolatry, or error to faith and guidance.", "reasons": "Qatada, Mujahid and others use error/guidance; Ibn Abbas and Muqatil use shirk or unbelief/faith. {"id": "14:1/q15", "question": "Why are darknesses plural and light singular?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q15/p1", "position": "Error and false worship have many paths, while truth and guidance have one.", "reasons": "Razi, Tabatabai and Islahi contrast divergent desires and many paths with one truth; Alusi specifies multiple alleged deities versus tawhid. {"id": "14:1/q16", "question": "What inward movements do darkness and light depict?", "turns_on": "Which inward states the spatial imagery represents.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q16/p1", "position": "From multiplicity and created nature through veils to unity and the divine essence.", "reasons": "Qashani gives three paired readings; Alusi repeats them; Bursevi describes bodily and spirit worlds and seventy thousand veils of light and darkness, with humans uniquely capable of passing through them by God's guardianship and the Prophet and Quran as means, citing 2:257. {"id": "14:1/q17", "question": "What does 'by their Lord's permission' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether permission names legal authorization, foreknowledge, gracious facilitation, or God's effective decree and creation.", "positions": [{"id": "14:1/q17/p1", "position": "By God's command or authorization to teach and carry out the mission.", "reasons": "Nahas calls idhn figurative command; Dahhak, Muqatil and Abu Ali give command.
